segments.english: He wiped out every living thing that was on the surface of the ground, from humans to animals, to crawling things, and to the birds of the sky; they were wiped out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those with him in the ark.
segments.literal: and-wiped-out [object-marker] all-of the-living-thing which on face-of the-ground from-human to animal to crawler and-to bird-of the-sky and-were-wiped-out from-the-earth and-was-left only Noah and-which with-him in-the-ark

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of מחה. The subject, God, is not stated. Rashi: the form is Qal (like וַיִּפֶן, וַיִּבֶן), pointed with ḥireq under the yod, and not Niphal.
construct state
יְקוּם is rare: whatever stands or has existence.
construct; פְּנֵי is plural in form (the idiom 'face of the ground').
אָדָם without the article: humankind in general.
רֶמֶשׂ: what creeps or moves along the ground.
construct state
Niphal wayyiqtol, plural; answers the Qal וַיִּמַח.
Niphal wayyiqtol of שאר; the singular verb agrees with the nearer subject, Noah.

phrases.literal: '[object-marker] all-of the-living-thing'; the marker has no English counterpart.

phrases.english: that was on the surface of the ground
from humans to animals, to crawling things, and to the birds of the sky
phrases.literal: 'from-human to animal to crawler and-to bird-of the-sky'; the four classes of 7:21-22 restated.

phrases.english: they were wiped out from the earth
and those with him in the ark

grammar: וַיִּמַח (Qal) and וַיִּמָּחוּ (Niphal) are the same root: the act and its result stand side by side.
The two ordinals of the list are marked by the repeated עַד, and the last עַד takes ו: 'up to ... up to ... and up to'.
The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ closes the first half; the tevir on נֹחַ joins 'only Noah' to what follows.
אַךְ limits the survivors to Noah and those with him; the verb וַיִּשָּׁאֶר is singular.
segments.note: The English keeps the double verb (wiped out ... were wiped out) as the Hebrew has it. The parse in the pack gives Qal for the first verb, in agreement with Rashi.

commentary.summary: Rashi: וַיִּמַח is an active (Qal) form, not Niphal, like וַיִּפֶן and וַיִּבֶן from roots ending in he, pointed with ḥireq under the yod. The English has an active verb with God understood.
Rashi: אַךְ נֹחַ means 'Noah alone', and that is the plain sense; he adds the homily that Noah groaned and spat blood from the work of tending the animals, or that a lion bit him.

Ibn Ezra: וַיִּמָּחוּ מִן הָאָרֶץ means that their names were wiped out from the earth, since they left no offspring; וַיִּשָּׁאֶר means only Noah and those with him remained, a full answer to those who say the flood was not over all the earth.
Ramban: the doubling may stress that no eggs or nests of birds and creeping things were left; the rabbis read 'wiped out' for this world and 'from the earth' for the world to come.

apparatus: 7:23.20 vowels: WLC reads וַיִשָּׁאֶר without the dagesh in yod; the base text וַיִּשָּׁאֶר is followed.

segments.english: The waters prevailed over the earth for a hundred and fifty days.
segments.literal: and-prevailed the-waters upon the-earth fifty and-hundred-of day

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, plural; מַיִם takes a plural verb.
מַיִם is plural in form only.
מְאַת is the construct of מֵאָה: 'hundred of'.

phrases.english: for a hundred and fifty days
phrases.literal: 'fifty and-hundred-of day': the smaller number comes first, with the singular noun.

grammar: The merkha on וַיִּגְבְּרוּ and the tipḥa on הַמַּיִם lead to the etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ; the duration is a separate clause-end.
The number is written smaller number first: חֲמִשִּׁים וּמְאַת יוֹם, with the noun in the singular.
גָּבַר 'be strong' is used of waters 'gaining the upper hand'.
segments.note: 'Prevailed' keeps the sense of strength, not only rising. Ibn Ezra's point is about how the water gained: the springs broke open, and the rain fell intermittently.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: since the springs had burst open, the rain also fell one day and stopped one day, reading אָנֹכִי מַמְטִיר as continuous, as the later וַיִּכָּלֵא הַגֶּשֶׁם shows. This concerns the rain's pattern, not the wording of the verse.
Radak: the hundred and fifty days follow the forty, from 29 Kislev to 1 Sivan; a calendar calculation.

segments.english: God remembered Noah and every living creature and all the domestic animals that were with him in the ark, and God made a wind pass over the earth, and the waters subsided.
segments.literal: and-remembered God [object-marker] Noah and-[object-marker] all-of the-living-thing and-[object-marker] all-of the-beast which with-him in-the-ark and-made-pass God wind upon the-earth and-subsided the-waters

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of זכר; 'remember' of God means to act on what he has pledged.
construct state
חַיָּה: the living creatures other than domestic animals; Ibn Ezra includes beasts of the field, birds and creeping things.
construct state
בְּהֵמָה: domestic animals as against the wild חַיָּה.
Hiphil wayyiqtol of עבר: causative, 'made pass'. The pack lists no Hiphil sense for עָבַר.
רוּחַ: wind; Rashi reads a wind of comfort, an echo of the 'spirit' of 1:2.
wayyiqtol of שׁכך; Rashi and Ibn Ezra: they settled down and stopped rising, like the anger of the king in Esther 2:1 and 7:10.

phrases.english: that were with him in the ark
and God made a wind pass over the earth
phrases.literal: 'and-made-pass God wind upon the-earth': Hiphil, causative.

grammar: וַיִּזְכֹּר is not a lapse corrected: Radak says memory and forgetting do not apply to God; the Torah speaks in human terms, and the word means he acted for them.
The Hiphil וַיַּעֲבֵר makes God the cause: he made a wind pass; the qadma and merkha divide the clause.
The pashta twice on רוּחַ marks the word as a doubled accent (pashta, pashta) before the zaqef qaton on הָאָרֶץ.
וַיָּשֹׁכּוּ is from שׁכך; its stem and root meaning differ from שׂכך of Esther 7:10 only in spelling, and it has the sense 'settle, abate'.
segments.note: The English keeps 'God' for אֱלֹהִים by decision, even though Rashi reads it as the attribute of justice turned to mercy. 'Noah' stands for Noah with his sons and wives, as Ibn Ezra says. 'Wind' (not 'spirit') because the verb is Hiphil of 'pass over' and the object is something that blows over the earth; Rashi's 'wind of comfort' is recorded.

commentary.summary: Rashi: this name, אֱלֹהִים, is the attribute of justice, turned to mercy by the prayer of the righteous; the wickedness of the wicked turns mercy to justice. A homily on the divine name.
Rashi: what did God remember for the animals? Their merit, that they had not corrupted their ways before and had not used the ark. A homily.
Rashi: a wind of comfort and relief passed before him. The English has a wind and leaves the intention in the note.
Rashi: עַל הָאָרֶץ means concerning the affairs of the earth. The English reads the plain 'over the earth'.
Rashi: וַיָּשֹׁכּוּ is like כְּשֹׁךְ חֲמַת הַמֶּלֶךְ, a word for the settling of anger. The English: subsided.
Ibn Ezra: his sons and the women are included in Noah, who is the main one. The English names Noah.
Ibn Ezra: it includes beasts of the field, birds, and every creeping thing; the sense of 'remembered' is the oath God swore to Noah. The English has 'every living creature'.
Ibn Ezra: he made it pass continually. The English has the causative verb without an end point.

Ibn Ezra: they rested and no longer prevailed; so too the king's anger subsided (Esther 7:10); the dagesh in the kaf stands for a missing ayin, and both verbs are Qal. The English: the waters subsided.
Ramban: the mention of Noah is for his merit; the mention of the animals is not for merit but because God remembered his word at the creation and wished the species to continue.
Radak: the wind stood against the water so that it could no longer rise, and the water settled and went down by its nature.

segments.english: The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the sky were shut, and the rain from the sky was held back.
segments.literal: and-were-shut springs-of deep and-sluices-of the-sky and-was-held-back the-rain from-the-sky

tokens.note: Niphal wayyiqtol, plural, of סכר; Ibn Ezra: the same as 'were closed'.
construct state
תְּהוֹם: the primeval water below the earth (7:11).
אֲרֻבָּה: a lattice or sluice; construct plural.
Niphal wayyiqtol of כלא: shut up, restrain.

phrases.english: The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the sky were shut
phrases.literal: 'and-were-shut springs-of deep and-sluices-of the-sky': one verb for two subjects.

phrases.english: and the rain from the sky was held back

grammar: Both subjects of וַיִּסָּכְרוּ are in the construct (מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם, אֲרֻבֹּת הַשָּׁמַיִם); the verb is plural and agrees with the nearer.
Two Niphal wayyiqtols (וַיִּסָּכְרוּ, וַיִּכָּלֵא) describe the end of the flood as passives: no agent is named.
The Hebrew has no 'all' here, unlike 7:11 (כָּל מַעְיְנֹת): Rashi draws the lesson from this.
סכר and סגר are two forms of one meaning (Ibn Ezra, Radak).
segments.note: 'Floodgates' renders אֲרֻבֹּת, the word of 7:11. 'Shut' is chosen for סכר to match 'closed' of Ibn Ezra; 'stopped up' is the alternative.

commentary.summary: Rashi: when they opened, the text has כָּל מַעְיְנֹת; here it has no כָּל, for those useful to the world were left, such as the hot springs of Tiberias. The English likewise has no 'all'.
Rashi: וַיִּכָּלֵא means was held back, as in לֹא תִכְלָא רַחֲמֶיךָ (Psalm 40) and לֹא יִכְלֶה מִמְּךָ (Genesis 23).
Ibn Ezra: וַיִּסָּכְרוּ is like וַיִּסָּגְרוּ; kaf does not interchange with gimel, rather these are two roots with one meaning.
Ibn Ezra: it was shut up inside the storehouse. The English: held back.
Ramban: no more rain fell until they left the ark; the heavens were like iron.

segments.english: The waters withdrew from the earth steadily, and the waters decreased at the end of a hundred and fifty days.
segments.literal: and-returned the-waters from-upon the-earth going and-returning and-decreased the-waters from-end-of fifty and-hundred-of day

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of שׁוב: 'return', here 'go back' from the earth.
מֵעַל: a compound preposition, 'from on top of'.
infinitive absolute of הלך: the continuous or repeated action; the sense of the stem here is 'go on'.
infinitive absolute of שׁוב; הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב is the idiom for 'steadily, to and fro'.
wayyiqtol of חסר, 'be lacking, diminish'.
מִקְצֵה: construct, 'from the end of'.
construct of מֵאָה

phrases.english: The waters withdrew from the earth

phrases.literal: 'going and-returning': a pair of infinitive absolutes showing continuing action.

phrases.english: at the end of a hundred and fifty days

grammar: הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב: two infinitive absolutes after a finite verb express continuing action (compare 8:5, הָלוֹךְ וְחָסוֹר).
The tevir on הַמַּיִם and the etnaḥta on וָשׁוֹב divide the verse after the first clause; the zaqef gadol on מִקְצֵה sets the number apart.
וַיַּחְסְרוּ is a stative Qal wayyiqtol of a verb with a stative vowel (חָסֵר).
The word order of the second clause puts the verb before its subject: וַיַּחְסְרוּ הַמַּיִם.
segments.note: 'Steadily' translates the idiom; the words 'going and returning' are in the literal line. The English follows the timing of Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak: the waters began to decrease at the end of the hundred and fifty days. Ramban joins מִקְצֵה with the following 'the ark came to rest'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: they began to decrease on the first of Sivan. How? The rains stopped on 27 Kislev; there are three more of Kislev, twenty-nine of Tevet, and so on to one hundred and fifty.

Ibn Ezra: וַיָּשֻׁבוּ means below the earth as usual, at the end of the hundred and fifty days; he rejects the attempts to compute the months by the sun or by intercalation. The English: steadily, at the end of the days.
Radak: little by little, until they decreased at the end of a hundred and fifty days; they began to decrease on 1 Sivan, when the rising stopped.
Ramban: the waters were decreasing little by little until the ground was dry; the words מִקְצֵה חֲמִשִּׁים וּמְאַת יוֹם join to וַתָּנַח הַתֵּבָה: on that day the decrease was great.

segments.english: The ark came to rest in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on the mountains of Ararat.
segments.literal: and-rested the-ark in-the-month the-seventh in-seven-ten day of-the-month upon mountains-of Ararat

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, feminine singular, to agree with תֵּבָה; the root נוח 'rest' is also Noah's name.
שִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר: 'seven-ten', the way Hebrew says seventeen.
construct plural; 'mountains' may mean the region (sense 2).
a region name, 'Ararat'; the text says mountains of Ararat, not one mountain.

phrases.english: on the seventeenth day of the month

grammar: וַתָּנַח: the verb is feminine, as תֵּבָה is feminine; a play on נֹחַ, whose name comes from נוח.
The date has three parts: the month by ordinal (הַשְּׁבִיעִי), the day by cardinal (שִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם), and then 'of the month'.
The zaqef qaton on הַשְּׁבִיעִי and the etnaḥta on לַחֹדֶשׁ separate the date from the place.
segments.note: The English does not say which reckoning gives 'the seventh month'. Rashi and Radak count from the stopping of the rain (Sivan); Ramban attributes another reckoning to Ibn Ezra and others. Rashi's inference that the ark sank eleven cubits is a calculation from the days and cubits.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the seventh month is Sivan, the seventh from the stopping of the rains in Kislev. The English leaves the starting point of the count open.

Rashi: from here you learn that the ark was sunk eleven cubits in the water, by a calculation from the exposure of the mountain tops at a rate of one cubit in four days. A computation that does not bear on the words.
Ramban: rejects Rashi's counts as not suiting the wording and says the sinking is not proved.
Radak: the seventh month is Sivan, the seventh from the rain's stopping; the ark rested on the seventeenth of it.
Radak: the mountains of Ararat may be the high ones, or the ark was in that region; some are lower, since not all were seen until the tenth month.

segments.english: The waters continued to diminish steadily until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains became visible.
segments.literal: and-the-waters were going and-diminishing until the-month the-tenth in-the-tenth on-one to-the-month were-seen heads-of the-mountains

tokens.note: perfect, plural of היה with infinitive absolutes: a continuous 'kept on'.
infinitive absolute of הלך
infinitive absolute of חסר, 'be lacking, diminish'; הָלוֹךְ וְחָסוֹר 'ever decreasing'.
'on one of the month': the first day of the month.
perfect, plural, Niphal of ראה
construct plural of רֹאשׁ: the heads of the mountains.

phrases.english: The waters continued to diminish steadily
in the tenth month, on the first day of the month
the tops of the mountains became visible

grammar: הָיוּ הָלוֹךְ וְחָסוֹר: the finite verb 'be' with two infinitive absolutes gives the sense 'kept on diminishing'.
The tenth month is named twice, in the ordinal with and without the preposition (עַד הַחֹדֶשׁ הָעֲשִׂירִי; בָּעֲשִׂירִי).
The date uses בְּאֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ for 'on the first of the month', with ל for 'of'.
נִרְאוּ is the Niphal 'appeared, was seen'; the subject רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים is plural.
segments.note: 'Became visible' for Niphal of ראה. Radak: they did not all go down until the land was seen; the mountain tops were first seen in the tenth month and the decrease continued after.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the tenth is Av, the tenth from Marheshvan, when the rain began; the seventh month he counts from the stopping, but the tenth cannot be counted from the stopping. The English leaves the count open.

Ibn Ezra: Noah fixed the first of the month without seeing the moon, since the window was not yet open; the tenth month is counted from the day of the flood, and he sent the raven on the tenth of Shevat. The English leaves the reckoning open.
Radak: they kept diminishing, as in 'the creatures ran and returned' (Ezekiel 1:14).
Radak: it does not say all the water was gone in the tenth month; only the tops of the mountains were seen then, and the decrease went on after.
Ramban: the order is inverted: the waters kept diminishing until the mountain tops were seen in the tenth month, which is Tammuz.

segments.english: At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made.
segments.literal: and-it-was from-end-of forty day and-opened Noah [object-marker] window-of the-ark which he-made

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of היה as a time formula: 'and it came to pass'.
מִקֵּץ: construct, 'at the end of'.
wayyiqtol of פתח
חַלּוֹן: construct; the same as the צֹהַר of 6:16 (Rashi, Radak).
perfect of עשׂה: the window made earlier, hence the pluperfect in English.

phrases.english: At the end of forty days
phrases.literal: 'and-it-was from-end-of forty day': the narrative formula וַיְהִי with a time phrase.

grammar: וַיְהִי with a time phrase begins a new episode: 'at the end of forty days'.
The zaqef gadol on וַיְהִי and the etnaḥta on יוֹם set the time clause apart from the main clause וַיִּפְתַּח נֹחַ.
אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה is a perfect that refers back to 6:16: 'which he had made'.
segments.note: 'The window' is the opening of 6:16 (צֹהַר). The starting point of the forty days is not given by the Hebrew: Rashi counts from the sight of the tops of the mountains; Radak prefers from the ark's coming to rest.

commentary.summary: Rashi: from the time the mountain tops were seen. The English leaves the starting point of the forty days open.
Rashi: the window is for the light-opening (צֹהַר), and not the ark's door made for entering and leaving. The English: window.
Radak: the forty days are from when the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat, since Noah could not have known when the water began to decrease, but felt the ark rest on something solid.
Radak: it is the צֹהַר of 6:16, and from it he sent the raven; he waited because he feared the waves would come in through it.
